name: When Trial AI Needs FDA Credibility Evidence
blurb: Which trial uses of AI fall under the FDA framework.
title: When Trial AI Needs FDA Credibility Evidence
answer: AI that produces data the FDA will rely on, for example to select patients, measure outcomes or support dosing, falls under the FDA's draft credibility framework. Purely operational uses such as drafting documents or scheduling sites generally do not, though the sponsor still owns the result.

reading.body:
The FDA's draft credibility framework applies to AI that produces data the agency will rely on, not to operational tools like scheduling or document drafting.

The dividing line is whether an AI output feeds a regulatory decision on safety, effectiveness or quality. Patient selection, outcome measurement and dosing support sit on the regulated side. Back office and site coordination work sits outside the framework, but the sponsor still owns the result either way.

For clinical teams the practical consequence is timing. Sorting trial AI into decision supporting and operational uses at the start determines which tools need the full credibility file and which do not, and that sort is cheaper to do before a model is in use than after.

The data covers one draft guidance and its scope. It does not say what evidence a credibility file must contain, how the FDA will review one, or when the draft becomes final.

sections.body: Sort trial AI into decision supporting and operational at the start; only the first needs the full credibility file.
